Group 1.text:
Review of BLUEPRINT.md and AGENTS.md
Overall Impression
Both documents are unusually thorough for a project of this scope. They read less like "docs" and more like an operational contract between the codebase and every future maintainer (human or AI). The level of specificity — named constants, exact migration timestamps, explicit "do not" lists, and cross-references to source files — is the right instinct for a system that handles regulatory compliance, money (Stripe), and owner-level disaster recovery.
That said, the two files together are approaching the length where they become a maintenance liability rather than a force multiplier. Below is a structured review.
BLUEPRINT.md — Architecture Reference
Strengths

    Entity definitions are self-contained. Each record type lists its fields, invariants, and the why behind non-obvious defaults (e.g., GrainMovement.bushels may be negative; HarvestRecord.landlordSplitPercent is pre-suggested from producerShare). This is the single most valuable thing in the file.
    The "Ghost Row" prevention rule for grain movements and the FSA/CLU upsert exception are called out as exceptions to general rules, which is exactly how conventions should be documented.
    Visual design system section is rare and valuable — most projects skip typography splits, radius standards, and dark-mode palette values. This will pay dividends when new contributors touch the UI.
    Owner DR section is honest about its state ("implemented tooling; deployment/drills pending"). That framing prevents the docs from overselling readiness.

Concerns

    Length without a table of contents. The file is ~900 lines with numbered sections but no anchor links. An AI agent (or human) searching for "grain concurrency" has to scan the whole file. A TOC at the top would cut first-read time in half.
    Some sections mix architecture with policy. Section 3 (Data Architecture) is pure schema. Section 4 (State Management) drifts into UI policy ("never use .delete() on user records"). That policy belongs in AGENTS.md or a dedicated "Rules" section.
    Migration timestamps are hardcoded. 20260715130000_backfill_plant_acreage_to_fsa_acreage.sql is referenced three times. If that migration is ever renamed or squashed, the blueprint goes stale. Prefer referencing the rule ("historical plant acreage was backfilled to FSA cropland") and letting the migration be an implementation detail.
    The "Future Expansion (Planned)" block under Weather Page is a roadmap fragment in an architecture doc. Either move it to a ROADMAP.md or clearly mark it as non-binding.

Suggestions

    Add a top-of-file TOC with anchor links.
    Split "State Management Rules" into invariants (keep in BLUEPRINT) and mutation procedure (move to AGENTS).
    Replace hardcoded migration filenames with semantic references ("the spray-treated-area backfill migration").
    Move the Weather "Future Expansion" block to a roadmap file.

AGENTS.md — Cross-Agent Operating Guide
Strengths

    The "Non-Negotiable Rules" section is excellent. It front-loads the things that, if violated, cause data loss or compliance failures. The ordering (Data Safety → Farm Scoping → Season Scoping → Mapper Discipline → Optimistic Updates → Supabase) mirrors the actual order an agent should think through a change.
    Explicit "do not" lists are rare and valuable. "Do not use upsert for updates," "Do not reintroduce floating/sticky bottom bars on the dashboard," "Do not add a global tar override" — these prevent the exact classes of bugs that agents tend to introduce.
    The "Change Workflow" section (Before / While / After editing) is the most actionable part of either document. It tells an agent what commands to run and in what order.
    Testing guidance distinguishes unit vs. integration and explains why live-network tests are isolated. This prevents agents from accidentally adding flaky tests to the default suite.

Concerns

    Heavy duplication with BLUEPRINT. The optimistic update pattern, farm scoping rule, FSA/CLU upsert exception, grain movement concurrency guard, and AI disclaimer decision each appear 2–3 times across the two files. This creates three problems:
        Maintenance burden: a rule change requires editing multiple places.
        Drift risk: one copy gets updated, the others don't.
        Context bloat: agents load the same rule multiple times, eating into their context window.
    Some rules are stated but not enforced. "Never hard-delete user farm records" is a policy. A lint rule or TypeScript type that makes .delete() a compile error would be stronger. The docs should note where enforcement is code-level vs. convention-level.
    The AI disclaimer decision is repeated three times (BLUEPRINT §5, AGENTS §AI Assistant, AGENTS §Intentional product decision). Once is enough — pick the canonical location and reference it.
    File references assume a stable directory layout. @/lib/mappers.ts, @/store/useFsaTracts.ts, etc. are referenced by path. If the project reorganizes, dozens of references break. Consider grouping references by concept ("the FSA tract store") with a single canonical path listed once.
    The "Important Reference Files" list is 30+ entries. That's too many for an agent to hold in context. Split into "always read" (5–7 files) and "read when relevant" (the rest).

Suggestions

    Deduplicate aggressively. For each rule that appears in both files, pick one canonical location (usually BLUEPRINT for architecture, AGENTS for procedure) and have the other file link to it with a one-line summary.
    Add a "Canonical Locations" table at the top of AGENTS.md mapping each rule to its single source of truth.
    Shorten the "Important Reference Files" list to the 7 files an agent should always know about; move the rest to a "When Relevant" section.
    Note where rules are code-enforced. E.g., "The soft-delete rule is enforced by RLS policies that omit DELETE grants; client code must also filter deleted_at IS NULL."

Cross-Document Concerns
Issue
	
Impact
	
Recommendation
Same rule documented in both files
	
Drift risk, context bloat
	
Pick one canonical location per rule; the other file links to it
No version or "last reviewed" date
	
Agents can't tell if docs are current
	
Add a <!-- last-reviewed: 2026-09-22 --> header to each file
No explicit "what changed since last review"
	
Agents can't prioritize what to re-read
	
Add a #### Recent Changes section at the top of each file
Owner DR status is "pending" but documented in detail
	
Agents may treat it as live
	
Add a prominent ⚠️ NOT YET DEPLOYED banner at the top of that section
Testing commands are listed but not explained
	
Agents may run the wrong command
	
Add a one-line "what this does" next to each npm run command
Top 5 Recommendations (Priority Order)

    Add a TOC and "last reviewed" date to both files. Low effort, high payoff for navigation and freshness signals.
    Deduplicate the optimistic update pattern, farm scoping rule, and FSA/CLU upsert exception. Keep the full explanation in BLUEPRINT; AGENTS should link to it with a one-line summary.
    Shorten AGENTS.md's "Important Reference Files" list to 7 files; move the rest to a secondary section.
    Add a #### Recent Changes section at the top of each file, listing the last 3–5 substantive edits with dates. This lets agents skip re-reading sections that haven't changed.
    Move the Weather "Future Expansion" block and the AI disclaimer decision (keep only one copy) out of the core architecture sections to reduce noise.

Final Assessment
Both documents are strong — significantly better than what most projects produce. The specificity, the explicit "do not" lists, and the honest framing of incomplete features (owner DR) are all signs of a mature engineering culture.
The main risk is maintenance burden from duplication and length. If the team commits to deduplication and adds lightweight freshness signals (TOC, dates, recent-changes log), these files will remain authoritative for a long time. If not, they'll gradually drift, and agents will start trusting stale rules.
Grade: A− — excellent content, needs structural hygiene to stay maintainable.
